introduction-not-just-for-docker-images.core: Modern registries are universal warehouses for every build output (images, Helm charts, binaries, SBOMs, signatures, ML models), with proxying, retention and provenance.

first_principles.problem: Teams scatter artifacts across S3 buckets, CI storage and ad-hoc servers, with no lifecycle or trust.
truths: Artifacts need versioning, discovery and cleanup.
derivation: Store everything as **OCI artifacts** where possible.

analogy.title: A factory's central warehouse
analogy.story: Every finished product is labelled, shelved, tracked and eventually cleared out.
analogy.breaks: A central registry becomes critical infrastructure, so it needs HA and backups.

example.title: Consolidating artifacts

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One place to find, trust and clean up.

example.outcome: artifacts are managed as a product.

check.q: What kinds of artifacts can a modern OCI registry store?
check.a: Container images plus Helm charts, binaries, SBOMs, signatures, WASM modules and ML models.

oci-artifacts-the-generic-envelope.core: The OCI distribution spec isn't image-specific. Any content can be pushed as blobs with a manifest and a media type (Helm charts, WASM, SBOMs), and referrers link related artifacts like signatures to an image.

first_principles.problem: Each artifact type traditionally needed its own server (Helm repos, Maven, file shares).
truths: Media types describe what a blob is.
Existing auth and replication can be reused.
derivation: Push with **ORAS** or the native tool (`helm push oci://`).
Attach **referrers** (signatures, SBOMs) to a subject digest.

analogy.title: A standard shipping container
analogy.story: Designed for ships, but the same box goes on trucks and trains, carrying anything.
analogy.breaks: Not all registries fully support artifact types or the referrers API yet.

example.title: Pushing a Helm chart and a config bundle

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One registry serves charts, configs and images.

code.text:
helm push mychart-1.2.0.tgz oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts
oras push ghcr.io/acme/config:v3 ./config.tar.gz:application/vnd.acme.config.v1+tar

example.outcome: a single distribution system for everything.

check.q: What does the OCI referrers API enable?
check.a: Linking artifacts such as signatures and SBOMs to the image digest they describe.

universal-package-managers-the-proxy-cac.core: A universal artifact manager proxies and caches upstream registries (npm, PyPI, Maven, Docker Hub), so builds survive upstream outages or deletions, run faster, avoid rate limits and pass through policy checks.

first_principles.problem: When left-pad was unpublished from npm in 2016, thousands of builds broke instantly, and Docker Hub rate limits stall CI.
truths: Upstream registries can fail, delete or rate-limit.
A local copy removes that dependency.
derivation: Point every client at **virtual repos** (proxy + internal).
Host **internal packages** in the same place.

analogy.title: A local library branch
analogy.story: Books from the central library are copied locally, so readers aren't stranded when the central branch closes.
analogy.breaks: Cached copies of malicious packages persist, so you need the ability to purge and block.

example.title: Docker Hub rate limits
flow: CI pulls node:20 via Harbor proxy
example.outcome: builds no longer depend on public uptime.

check.q: What incident illustrates the need for proxy caches?
check.a: The 2016 left-pad unpublishing that broke builds across the npm ecosystem.

retention-policies-hoarding-vs-cleaning.core: High-velocity CI produces terabytes of artifacts. Retention policies delete what's unneeded (old PR builds, untagged images) while protecting releases and anything currently deployed.

first_principles.problem: 50 PRs a day × 500 MB images grows storage costs without bound, and registries slow down.
truths: Most build artifacts are never used again.
Releases and deployed artifacts must be kept.
derivation: **Keep**: release tags, what's deployed, the last N per branch.
**Expire**: PR and untagged images after X days.

analogy.title: Cleaning out a warehouse
analogy.story: Keep the flagship products and current stock; clear out prototypes and expired samples on a schedule.
analogy.breaks: Deleting an image a running pod still uses breaks rescheduling, so check what's deployed.

example.title: An ECR lifecycle policy

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Storage stays flat while releases are preserved.

example.outcome: controlled costs without losing what matters.

check.q: What must a retention policy never delete?
check.a: Release artifacts and anything currently deployed or needed for rollback.

artifact-signing-and-provenance.core: A registry tells you where an artifact is, not whether to trust it. Signatures and provenance attestations, stored as referrers next to the artifact, let consumers verify origin and build integrity before use.

first_principles.problem: A compromised CI credential pushes a malicious artifact under a legitimate tag.
truths: Write access to the registry isn't proof of legitimacy.
Cryptographic signatures bind content to an identity.

analogy.title: Tamper-evident seals on warehouse goods
analogy.story: Storage location doesn't prove authenticity, but an intact manufacturer's seal does.
analogy.breaks: Signing keys and identities must be protected, or attackers sign their own artifacts.

example.title: Rejecting a tampered tag
flow: No valid signature from CI identity

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Registry compromise doesn't become a cluster compromise.

check.q: Why isn't 'it's in our registry' enough to trust an artifact?
check.a: Anyone with registry write access, such as a compromised credential, could have pushed it.
